title: About Onim
excerpt: A free library of 4,000+ calculators and file tools, built so that every answer comes with the working that produced it.
content:
Onim is a free library of calculators and browser tools. You type a number or drop in a file, you get an answer, and the page shows the formula or the method that produced it. There is no account, no paywall and no “unlock the result” step. If a page cannot explain how it reached its answer, that page is not finished.

What is here

The site is organised in fifteen sections — from Biology and Chemistry to Design & CSS and Text & Writing — and holds two kinds of tool:

  • Calculators. A page with inputs, a result and the equation it used. Roughly four thousand of them: percentages, loans, units, health, geometry, date arithmetic and a great deal of science.
  • File tools. Converters, compressors, resizers, encoders and formatters that work on a file you hand them — an image, a PDF, a spreadsheet. The file is processed in the page; it is never uploaded to a server.

How a page is built

Each calculator is described by the relationships between its inputs. Those equations are what the page runs on — once on the server while the page is drawn, and again in your browser the moment you press Calculate, so the two can be compared. Where a problem needs more than arithmetic (a table lookup, an iterative solve, a piecewise rule, a tax band), that logic is written out step by step instead of being hidden in a black box.

Every page carries the same furniture, because a result without context is not much use: the formula with its variables defined, a worked example with real numbers, the assumptions the answer rests on, a table of neighbouring results, and the questions people ask about it.

How the answers are checked

Each calculator is tested against worked examples whose results are stated independently of the code: the answer is computed by hand or taken from an authoritative source, then the page has to reproduce it. A calculator that disagrees with its worked example is a bug, and it is fixed rather than annotated. File tools are tested on files with known properties — a 1200 pixel image that has to come back 1200 pixels wide, a PDF whose page count must not change.

What happens to what you type

Calculations run in your browser and on this server while the page is being drawn. We do not store your inputs, we do not build profiles, and we do not sell data to anyone. Uploaded files are read in your browser and never leave it. The only information we keep is what you deliberately send — a message through the contact form — and we keep that only as long as it takes to answer it. The privacy policy spells this out in detail.

How the site is paid for

Onim is free to use and costs money to run. It is funded by advertising: a small number of clearly marked placements, never inside a result and never between you and an answer. Advertisers do not see your inputs, cannot influence a result, and get no access to the calculators. If advertising is turned off on this deployment, nothing else changes.

Who builds it

Onim is written and maintained by a small independent team. The calculators exist because people kept needing one more of them: a conversion no site explained, a formula buried in a textbook, a tool that wanted an account for a two-second job. If something is missing, ask for it — requests from readers are where a good share of the library came from.

Getting in touch

Bug reports, corrections and requests all go to the same place. The contact page has the form and says what makes a report easy to act on. If a result looks wrong, the calculator name, the values you entered and the answer you expected is usually enough to reproduce it.
